theory.title: Pre-Norm Attention for the First Token
overview: Rebuild the running example's block as pre-norm, with the same weights: attention reads $\text{LayerNorm}(H)$, and its output is added to $H$ itself, with no LayerNorm after the addition.
In the running example the causal mask lets the first token attend only to itself, and $W_V$ and $W_O$ leave a vector unchanged.

prompt.p: What is the vector of "the" after the attention part and its residual addition? Give its length to three decimal places.

answer.p: "the" is the first token, so the mask leaves it only itself to look at, with weight 1 in both heads. Its attention output is therefore its own value, and in pre-norm the values are made from the normalized copy. $W_V$ and $W_O$ both leave a vector unchanged, so the output is $\text{LayerNorm}$ of the row of "the", $(1, 1, 0, 1)$:
The residual adds this to $H$ itself:

In the post-norm block of this page, "the" leaves the same step with length 2, because a LayerNorm follows every addition. In pre-norm nothing normalizes the sum, so the vector carried to the next part is longer, and each later part adds to it again. That is why GPT-2 ends with a final LayerNorm.

Three slips give other lengths. Normalizing after the addition, as in post-norm, gives 2. Adding the output to the normalized copy instead of to $H$ gives $2 \times (0.577, 0.577, -1.732, 0.577)$, of length 4. Letting attention read $H$ itself gives $2H$, of length 3.464.

theory.title: The Weights That Learn from One Token
overview: Training on the loss at the second position, where "cat" predicts "sat", sends a gradient back into the feed-forward network of "cat", whose input is the row of "cat" in $Y$, $(-0.698,\ 1.677,\ -0.821,\ -0.158)$. Assume that the gradient reaching the network's output for "cat" has no zero entries. The two rules you need are in [Backpropagation by Hand](/module/?id=backpropagation-mechanics): a weight's gradient is the input it reads times the error at the unit it feeds, and the ReLU's slope is 1 where its input is positive and 0 elsewhere.

prompt.p: How many of the 32 weights in $W_1$ get a nonzero gradient from this loss?

answer.p: The eight hidden values of "cat", from the table of the running example:

answer.tex:
\begin{array}{cccc}
\text{Hidden value} & \text{Computed as} & \text{For "cat"} & \text{After the ReLU} \\ \hline
1 & \text{dim 1 − dim 4} & \text{−0.540} & 0 \\
2 & \text{dim 2} & 1.677 & 1.677 \\
3 & \text{dim 3} & \text{−0.821} & 0 \\
4 & \text{dim 4 − dim 1} & 0.540 & 0.540 \\
5 & \text{−dim 2} & \text{−1.677} & 0 \\
6 & \text{dim 1 − dim 3} & 0.123 & 0.123 \\
7 & \text{dim 2 − dim 4} & 1.835 & 1.835 \\
8 & \text{dim 3} & \text{−0.821} & 0
\end{array}

answer.p: Work back from the output. $W_2$ sends hidden value $j$ to output $j$ or $j - 4$ with a weight of $\pm\tfrac12$, so every hidden value after the ReLU gets a nonzero gradient. The ReLU passes that gradient on where its input was positive and blocks it where it was negative, because there its output stays 0 under a small change. So only the hidden values that are on, 2, 4, 6 and 7, pass a gradient back to their inputs.

Hidden value $j$ is $\sum_i y_i\,(W_1)_{ij}$, so the gradient of weight $(i, j)$ is $y_i$ times the gradient reaching hidden value $j$. All four numbers of the input are nonzero, so each of the 4 columns of the values that are on gets 4 nonzero entries: $4 \times 4 = 16$.

Hidden value 6 is on by only 0.123, and it still counts. The other 16 weights learn nothing from this position. The same count gives 8 for "sat", whose hidden values 4 and 5 are on. Taking six of the eight as off for every token, as for "sat", would give 8 here, and letting the gradient through every hidden value would give all 32.

theory.title: Counting the Weights of GPT-2 Large
overview: GPT-2 large keeps the design of GPT-2 small, its vocabulary of 50,257 tokens and its 1,024 positions, but has a width of 1,280, 20 heads of 64 numbers and 36 blocks. Its feed-forward network widens to four times the width.

prompt.p: How many weights does it have? Count everything this module's table counts, offsets included, and give the total in millions to two decimal places.

answer.p: First read off from GPT-2 small, with $d = 768$, how many offsets each part has:

list: Attention: $2{,}362{,}368 - 4 \times 768^2 = 3{,}072 = 4d$, one list of $d$ offsets for each of the four tables.
Feed-forward: $4{,}722{,}432 - 2 \times 768 \times 3{,}072 = 3{,}840 = 4d + d$, one offset per hidden value and one per output number.
LayerNorms: a scale and a shift of $d$ numbers each, twice, $4d$.

answer.p: So a block holds $4d^2 + 4d$ in attention, $8d^2 + 5d$ in the feed-forward network and $4d$ in its norms. With $d = 1{,}280$:

answer.tex:
\begin{array}{cc}
\text{Part} & \text{Weights} \\ \hline
\text{Token embeddings, $50{,}257 \times 1{,}280$} & \text{64,328,960} \\
\text{Position embeddings, $1{,}024 \times 1{,}280$} & \text{1,310,720} \\
\text{Attention, $4d^2 + 4d$} & \text{6,558,720} \\
\text{Feed-forward, $8d^2 + 5d$} & \text{13,113,600} \\
\text{Two LayerNorms, $4d$} & \text{5,120} \\
\text{One block} & \text{19,677,440} \\
\text{36 blocks} & \text{708,387,840} \\
\text{Final LayerNorm, $2d$} & \text{2,560} \\
\textbf{Total} & \textbf{774,030,080}
\end{array}

answer.p: That is 774.03 million, the figure usually quoted for GPT-2 large as 774M. The 20 heads do not enter the count: splitting the width into heads costs no weights (Step 8). Counting a separate output table would add another 64,328,960, for 838.36 million, and giving every head its own $1{,}280 \times 1{,}280$ tables would multiply the attention weights by 20. The blocks hold 92% of the weights here, against 68% in GPT-2 small, because they grow with $d^2$ and the embedding tables only with $d$.
